newsitem.title: FRANCE: Juppe says bowing out will help centre-right win.
newsitem.headline: Juppe says bowing out will help centre-right win.

text.p: French Prime Minister Alain Juppe said on Tuesday his plan to bow out would help the centre-right win re-election but the opposition Socialists said the government was floundering with neither policies nor leaders.

Juppe, stunned by a left-wing upset in the first round of parliamentary elections, said his departure after Sunday's runoff would give President Jacques Chirac new last-minute arguments to convince voters to re-elect the conservatives.

Juppe told RTL radio a centre-right victory was "probable" but conceded it was "possible" the left would win the runoff. He said he was sacrificing himself to help the centre-right push for change with new faces.

Chirac, basking in the glory of hosting a summit of NATO leaders and Russian President Boris Yeltsin on Tuesday, was due to address the nation on television at 8 p.m. (1800 GMT) in a bid to bolster his centre-right allies.

Socialist Party leader Lionel Jospin said that voters should "democratically turn the page" and that Juppe's departure underscored the disarray of the ruling coalition, made up of the Gaullist RPR and the centrist UDF.

"We already did not know what the policy of the RPR and the UDF was in this campaign, since they refused to accept their record, did not publish their plans and hid their intentions for the future," Jospin said.
"Now we don't even know who would lead this unknown policy," he told Europe 1 radio. Jospin has accused the centre-right of planning to tighten austerity after the poll.

The Paris stock market traded little changed on Tuesday morning after a 3.9 percent plunge on Monday on fears of a left-wing victory. Dealers said Juppe's self-sacrifice, announced after Monday's close, had had little impact on prices.
"Our feeling is that Juppe either resigned too late or too early. It's a joker but it has not been well played," said Olivier Blitz of IFF.

Juppe said he did not feel bitter but said he had been "a sort of scapegoat", doing the "dirty work" of reconciling Chirac's 1995 campaign promises of top priority for jobs with austerity policies to qualify for a single European currency.
Opinion polls last year showed that Juppe, who presided over austerity and record unemployment of 12.8 percent, was the least popular prime minister in France's 39-year-old Fifth Republic.
Far-right leader Jean-Marie Le Pen said Chirac had acted like a sea captain throwing an overweight passenger overboard because his ship was leaking.

Most commentators said Philippe Seguin, outgoing speaker of the National Assembly and one-time campaigner against the single European currency, was favourite to take over as premier if the centre-right won.

"Chirac dissolves Juppe," both the daily Le Parisien and Liberation said in front-page headlines. Under the French Fifth Republic, founded by General Charles de Gaulle, the president is all-powerful and his prime minister a safety fuse which can be allowed to burn out in the event of political unpopularity.

Chirac dissolved the National Assembly last month, calling for a "new elan" to help revitalise France for a single European currency and ensure himself a friendly majority until the end of his own term in 2002.

A left-wing victory would force Chirac to share power with a hostile prime minister, probably Jospin, making him a virtual lame duck. Late Socialist president Francois Mitterrand shared power twice with a conservative premier, in 1986-1988 and 1993-1995.

Jospin rebuffed Chirac for saying last week that France's voice in Europe would be weakened by cohabitation. "I don't doubt that the voice of France, after June 1, will resemble what has been said by the French people on June 1," he said.

Former European Commission president Jacques Delors, a Socialist, said the left would make qualifying for the euro single currency its top priority if it won even though Jospin has placed conditions on joining and ruled out extra austerity.
"Respecting the 1999 deadline for European economic and monetary union appears as an absolute obligation," Delors told the weekly Nouvel Observateur.
